title: Vectiq: Building a Community Bot for Vector
subtitle: How a real Python community-management bot is put together: SQLite, modules, cogs, economy, moderation, WebXDC games and plugins
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A beginner-friendly tour of Vectiq (github.com/lucky-edgelord/aio-vector-bot, MIT), a community-management bot for the Vector messenger written in Python on vector-sdk-py. In 13 chapters you learn what the bot does and how its code is organised: the layering rule (cogs for Vector, stores for SQL, pure rules for logic), the async SQLite database with transactions and migrations, the layered configuration, the module and slot system, cogs and commands, the leveling curve, the atomic economy, moderation and safety modules, verification with device checks, WebXDC games with the bot as referee, restore points, the dashboard and MCP, and finally testing with fakes and writing your own plugin. There are 26 numbered figures, 26 numbered tables, a recap, a memory trick, an expanded ELI5 and a concept map in every chapter, a final exam, and a handful of short Python labs that run offline in the app: the XP curve, daily streaks, durations, domain lists, migrations, config merging, device marks, tic-tac-toe and slot conflicts. Credits: the course is original and describes the open source project Vectiq by lucky-edgelord and the Vectiq contributors (MIT licence). The project credits Logiq and MEE6 for the feature shape, GateBot by henk.tech (MIT) for the verification ideas and Sentire by JSKitty of VectorPrivacy for automod. Vector is a trademark of its owners and is not affiliated with this course. Read the source at the repository to see the current code.

chapters.title: What Vectiq is and where it fits
summary: Vectiq is a community-management bot for Vector, the private messenger. It does what Discord bots such as MEE6 do for a server: moderation, levels, a coin economy, tickets, events, giveaways and games.

It is written in Python from scratch on top of vector-sdk-py, uses SQLite instead of a separate database server, and is MIT licensed by lucky-edgelord and the Vectiq contributors. This course walks through how it is built so you can run it, read it and extend it.
The big idea to remember: every feature is a module with its own cog (the Vector side), store (the database side) and settings. You switch modules on and off, and the rest stays out of the way.

chapters.title: The database: async SQLite, transactions and migrations
summary: SQLite is a database in one file. Python's sqlite3 module is blocking, so a naive bot would freeze whenever the database was busy. Vectiq wraps it in an async Database class: one shared connection, every call run in a worker thread, and a lock so calls take turns.
Transactions group several changes into one all-or-nothing step. The Database offers transaction(), which starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE and rolls back if your code raises an error.

Migrations are numbered SQL scripts. The database remembers how many it has run in PRAGMA user_version, so an old file upgrades itself at start-up. The golden rule: never edit a migration that has shipped, append a new one.

glossary.def: A group of statements that all succeed or all fail.
Write-ahead logging: readers and a writer can work at the same time.
A numbered SQL script that moves the schema one step forward.
A number stored inside the SQLite file; Vectiq uses it as the schema version.
Run blocking code in a worker thread so the event loop stays free.

keyPoints: One connection, one lock, every call in asyncio.to_thread.
Pragmas: WAL, foreign_keys ON, synchronous NORMAL, busy_timeout 5000.
transaction() uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE and rolls back on an exception.
Migrations apply in order, those newer than user_version.

ELI5. A diary with a lock. Only one person writes at a time, so nobody scribbles over each other. And if you start copying a list from one page to another, you either finish the whole copy or tear out what you did.

Now the real words. Vectiq uses SQLite through one shared connection, a lock, and worker threads so the bot never freezes. Transactions make several changes all-or-nothing, and numbered migrations upgrade an old diary to the new format.
Try it. Say what would go wrong if moving a coin from A to B stopped halfway.
If you remember one thing: A transaction means both changes happen or neither does.

chapters.title: Configuration: defaults, YAML, dashboard overrides and secrets

chapters.title: Cogs, commands, listeners and cooldowns
summary: A cog is a class that groups the commands, event listeners and background loops of one feature. Because Vectiq follows the discord.py style, anyone who has written a Discord bot will feel at home.
Each command can have checks, such as who may use it, and cooldowns, such as how often. When something goes wrong, on_command_error turns the failure into a friendly message instead of a crash.

Vector publishes commands as slash commands too, but only up to a limit of 64 native ones, so Vectiq tracks that limit. A group's checks are copied down to its subcommands, so one check protects them all.

chapters.title: Leveling: the XP curve and the level store

maps.title: Leveling
links: Level up | can give | Role reward

summary: Leveling rewards activity. Each message earns a random amount of XP, but only once per cooldown, so spamming does not help. Total XP decides your level.
Vectiq uses the MEE6 curve: the XP to climb from level n to n+1 is 5n squared plus 50n plus 100. The total to reach a level is the sum of those steps. A short loop turns XP into a level and back.
All the database work is in LevelStore; the cog only listens to messages, announces level-ups and draws rank cards with Pillow in a worker thread so the bot never lags.

glossary.def: Experience points earned by chatting.
A rank derived from total XP using the curve.
